CALIFORNIA UNIFORM SIMULTANEOUS DEATH ACT — GENERAL INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for —

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
California's Uniform Simultaneous Death Act — Probate Code Part 5 (§§ 220-234), Chapter 1, General Provisions (§§ 220-226) — sets the general default rule for how property passes when two or more people die at the same time, or when it cannot be established which of them died first. This information sheet explains that general statutory framework and its application to intestate succession, gifts conditioned on survivorship generally, joint tenancy, and community property. Two more specific default rules addressed elsewhere in this corpus are not repeated here: the 120-hour survival rule for a will beneficiary, covered in this corpus's Last Will and Testament document, and the simultaneous-death rule for a named life insurance beneficiary, covered in this corpus's Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation document.

THE GENERAL DEFAULT RULE WHEN PRIORITY OF DEATH CAN'T BE ESTABLISHED
California's Uniform Simultaneous Death Act sets a general default rule under Prob. Code § 220: except as otherwise provided elsewhere in the same chapter, if title to property or its devolution depends on which of two people died first, and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that one of them survived the other, each person's property is administered or distributed as if that person had survived the other. This baseline rule turns on a clear-and-convincing-evidence standard about who survived whom — it does not itself set a fixed 120-hour, or any other numeric, survival period. A specific survival-period requirement, where one applies, comes from a more specific statute outside or within this chapter, not from § 220 itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as otherwise provided in this chapter, if the title to property or the devolution of property depends upon priority of death and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that one of the persons survived the other, the property of each person shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, as if that person had survived the other."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 220, California Probate Code, general default rule when priority of death cannot be established (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=220.)
  Known gap: This is California's own general default provision, used as evidence of what the statute itself provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reader's property, and not a statement about how a court would resolve any actual case's evidence of who died first. Section 220 opens with the phrase "Except as otherwise provided in this chapter," meaning the more specific default rules addressed elsewhere in this clause set (gifts conditioned on survivorship generally, joint tenancy) and in this corpus's other documents (a will beneficiary's 120-hour rule, a life insurance beneficiary's rule) can and do displace this general rule for their particular subject matter — § 220 is the residual baseline, not necessarily the rule that ultimately controls a given asset. This is a single statutory section; no additional independent source was found for this citation.

HOW MORE SPECIFIC DEFAULT RULES RELATE TO THIS GENERAL RULE
This chapter's general default rule does not operate in isolation. Under Prob. Code § 221(a), the chapter containing §§ 220-226 does not apply at all in any case where Prob. Code § 103 (community or quasi-community property between spouses), § 6211 (a California statutory will), or § 6403 (intestate succession) applies — each of those is a separate statute with its own default rule, not simply a restatement of § 220. Section 6403's 120-hour survival requirement for intestate succession is one such distinct, separately triggered rule; it is not an application of § 220 itself, and the two are not interchangeable. Separately, under Prob. Code § 221(b), this chapter also does not apply where a trust, deed, insurance contract, or other governing document makes its own explicit provision for simultaneous death, a common-disaster clause, or a stated survival period different from this chapter's own default.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This chapter does not apply in any case where Section 103, 6211, or 6403 applies."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 221(a), California Probate Code, general chapter inapplicable where a more specific statute governs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=221.)
  Known gap: This is California's own statute describing how its general default rule relates to more specific default rules found elsewhere in the Probate Code — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reader's situation, and not a determination of which particular statute (§ 103, § 6211, or § 6403) applies to any actual asset or instrument. Only § 221(a) is quoted as a citation here; § 221(b) is deliberately not re-quoted because this corpus's Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation document (clause: Simultaneous Death of the Insured and a Beneficiary) already quotes it in full — this clause cross-references that existing quote rather than duplicating it. This clause likewise does not restate or re-verify the 120-hour text of § 6403(a), already quoted and verified in this corpus's Last Will and Testament document (clause: If a Beneficiary Dies at Nearly the Same Time); § 6403 is described here only to disclose, as § 221(a) itself confirms, that it is a genuinely distinct, separately triggered provision rather than an application of § 220 — this clause does not treat the two as the same rule. Prob. Code § 6211 (a California statutory will's own 120-hour provision) is named by § 221(a) but was not independently fetched or verified for this clause set, and this clause does not assume it is identical in scope to § 6403's intestate-succession rule; that specific question is left to this corpus's will-specific material rather than resolved here. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for the § 221(a) citation itself.

GIFTS CONDITIONED ON SURVIVORSHIP, GENERALLY
Beyond the baseline rule in § 220, Prob. Code § 222 sets a more specific default for a disposition of property that makes a beneficiary's right to it conditional on surviving another person. If it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that the beneficiary survived that other person, the beneficiary is deemed not to have survived them. Where two or more beneficiaries would each have taken the entire property only by surviving the others, and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that any one of them survived the rest, the property is instead divided into as many equal portions as there are beneficiaries, and each portion is administered or distributed as if that beneficiary had survived the others.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If property is so disposed of that the right of a beneficiary to succeed to any interest in the property is conditional upon surviving another person and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that the beneficiary survived the other person, the beneficiary is deemed not to have survived the other person."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 222(a), California Probate Code, a beneficiary deemed not to have survived where conditional survivorship can't be established (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=222.)
  "If property is so disposed of that one of two or more beneficiaries would have been entitled to the property if he or she had survived the others, and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that any beneficiary survived any other beneficiary, the property shall be divided into as many equal portions as there are beneficiaries and the portion of each beneficiary shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, as if that beneficiary had survived the other beneficiaries."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 222(b), California Probate Code, equal-portion division among mutually-conditioned beneficiaries (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=222.)
  Known gap: This is California's own statute governing conditional survivorship gifts generally — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific reader's trust, deed, or other instrument, and not a statement about how to word a survivorship condition. Prob. Code § 222(a) and (b) are two subsections of the same statutory section, not independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. This clause does not address the joint-tenancy-specific version of this same kind of rule, which Prob. Code § 223 states separately and which is addressed in a separate clause in this set rather than here.

JOINT TENANCY: DIVISION INTO EQUAL SHARES AT SIMULTANEOUS DEATH
California has a default rule specifically for property held in joint tenancy when the joint tenants die simultaneously, or when it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence which of them survived. Under Prob. Code § 223, "joint tenants" for this purpose includes anyone who owns property under circumstances entitling one or more of them to the whole of it on the others' death — a broader, functional definition rather than a formal-title-only one. If two joint tenants have died and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that one survived the other, the property is administered or distributed one-half as if one joint tenant had survived and one-half as if the other had survived — dividing what would otherwise have passed entirely to a survivor into two separate halves. If more than two joint tenants have died and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that any of them survived the others, the property is instead divided into as many equal portions as there are joint tenants, with each portion administered or distributed as if that joint tenant had survived the rest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "As used in this section, “joint tenants” includes owners of property held under circumstances that entitled one or more to the whole of the property on the death of the other or others."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 223(a), California Probate Code, definition of joint tenants for the simultaneous-death chapter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=223.)
  "If property is held by two joint tenants and both of them have died and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that one survived the other, the property held in joint tenancy shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, one-half as if one joint tenant had survived and one-half as if the other joint tenant had survived."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 223(b), California Probate Code, division into two equal halves between two joint tenants (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=223.)
  "If property is held by more than two joint tenants and all of them have died and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that any of them survived the others, the property held in joint tenancy shall be divided into as many portions as there are joint tenants and the share of each joint tenant shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, as if that joint tenant had survived the other joint tenants."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 223(c), California Probate Code, equal-portion division among more than two joint tenants (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=223.)
  Known gap: This is California's own statute, used as evidence of what the law provides for jointly held property specifically — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reader's property, and not a statement about how title to any actual jointly held asset should be recorded or transferred. Prob. Code § 223(a), (b), and (c) are three subsections of the same statutory section, not independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. This rule is distinct from, and stated separately from, this chapter's general rule for conditional survivorship gifts (§ 222) and its default rule for community or quasi-community property (§ 103), each addressed in a separate clause in this set.

COMMUNITY AND QUASI-COMMUNITY PROPERTY AT SIMULTANEOUS DEATH
California has a separate default rule specifically for community and quasi-community property when spouses die simultaneously. Under Prob. Code § 103, except as provided by § 224 (this corpus's separate clause on life insurance that is itself community property), if spouses die leaving community or quasi-community property and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that one spouse survived the other: one-half of the community property and one-half of the quasi-community property is administered or distributed as if one spouse had survived, and belonged to that spouse; and the other one-half is administered or distributed as if the other spouse had survived, and belonged to that spouse. The effect parallels the joint-tenancy division described elsewhere in this clause set — an equal, one-half-and-one-half split — rather than the whole passing to either spouse's estate alone.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as provided by Section 224, if spouses die leaving community or quasi-community property and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that one spouse survived the other: (a) One-half of the community property and one-half of the quasi-community property shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, as if one spouse had survived and as if that one-half belonged to that spouse."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 103(a), California Probate Code, community property default rule and the first equal half (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=103.)
  "The other one-half of the community property and the other one-half of the quasi-community property shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, as if the other spouse had survived and as if that one-half belonged to that spouse."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 103(b), California Probate Code, community property default rule's other equal half (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=103.)
  Known gap: This is California's own statute, used as evidence of what the law provides for community and quasi-community property specifically — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reader's marital property, and not a statement about which particular assets are, in fact, community, quasi-community, or separate property, which this clause does not determine. Prob. Code § 103(a) and (b) are two subsections of the same statutory section, not independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. Notably, § 103 is codified in Probate Code Part 1 (§§ 100-105), not in Part 5's simultaneous-death chapter (§§ 220-234) that contains §§ 220-223 addressed elsewhere in this clause set — it is a separate statute that Prob. Code § 221(a) cross-references as displacing that chapter for community property, and it carries its own internal carve-out to § 224 rather than to anything in §§ 220-223. This clause does not restate § 224's life-insurance-specific community-property provision, already addressed in this corpus's Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation document (clause: Simultaneous Death of the Insured and a Beneficiary).
